blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Work: If a constant force $\vec{F}$ is applied on a body and displaces it through displacement $\vec{s}$ then work done by $\vec{F}$ on the body is given by scalar product of $\vec{F}$ and $\vec{s}$.

$W=\vec{F} \cdot \vec{s}=Fs \operatorname{cos} \theta$

SI Unit of work : Joule (J)

Dimensions: = [ML2T–2]

Note: Work is scalar quantity, but it can be positive, negative or zero.

Nature of Work Done:

(1) Positive Work :If the angle is acute ($\theta$< 90°) then the work done is said to be positive

(2) Negative work :If the angle is obtuse ($\theta$> 90°) then the work is said to be negative

(3) Zero Work : Either Force or displacement  is  zero or $\theta = 90^\circ$

blocks.title: Example
blocks.question: A 10 Kg block placed on a rough horizontal floor is being pulled by a constant force of 50 N. Coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the floor is 0.4.Find the work done by Kinetic friction acting on the block over a displacement of 5 m.
blocks.answer:
F.B.D. of the block is shown here

Work done by the force of kinetic friction

$W_f = \vec{f} \cdot \vec{s}$

$W_f=\vec{f} \cdot \vec{s}=f s \operatorname{Cos} 180^{\circ}$

$W_f = -fs$=$-40\times 5$=$-200J$

modules.name: Work Done By a Variable Force

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Work Done by Variable Force: Variable Force means  force with changing direction or magnitude or both.

$W=$$\int_{r_1}^{r_2} \vec{F} \cdot (d\vec{r})$

Work done in terms of Rectangular Components:

$W_{A B}=\int_A^B\left(F_x \hat{i}+F_y \hat{j}+F_z \hat{k}\right) \cdot(d x \hat{i}+d y \hat{j}+d z \hat{k})=\int_{x_A}^{x_B} F_x d x+\int_{y_A}^{y_B} F_y d y+\int_{z_A}^{z_B} F_z d z$

Graphical Meaning of Work:

$W_{A B}=\int_A^B \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~F}} \cdot \mathrm{~d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~s}}$

Work Done By Spring Force:

$W_s = \frac{1}{2} k \left( x_i^2 - x_f^2 \right)$

Dependency on Frame Of Reference:

  • Force: Independent of the frame of reference, always has the same value.
  • Displacement: Depends on the frame of reference, can vary in different frames.
  • Work: Depends on the frame of reference, due to dependency of displacement on frame.
Example:

  • In the lift's reference frame, the man's force is equal to the weight of the bag, but the displacement of the bag is zero, so the work done is zero.
  • In the ground's reference frame, the bag moves with the lift, so the force applied by man does non-zero work.
  • joule : One joule of work is said to be done when a force of one newton displaces a body by one meter in the direction of force.
$1 \text { joule = } 1 \text { newton } \times 1 \text { meter }=1 \mathrm{~kg}-\mathrm{m}^2 / \mathrm{s}^2$

$\text { (a) } 1 \text { joule }=10^7 \text { ergs }$

$\text { (b) } 1 \mathrm{erg}=10^{-7} \text { ioules }$

Examples of zero work:

• Body moving with uniform velocity. (F=0)
    • Net force on the particle is zero. ( F=0)
    • We push the wall and it remains at rest. (s=0)

• Satellite is moving around the earth.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Energy: It is defined as the internal capacity to do work. When we say that a body has energy it means that it can do work.

Different forms of energy: Mechanical energy, electrical energy, optical (light) energy, acoustical (sound), molecular, atomic and nuclear energy etc., are various forms of energy. These forms of energy can change from one form to the other.

• Energy is a scalar quantity

• Dimensions : [M1L2T–2]

• SI Unit : joule

1 erg = 10–7 J

Mechanical energy, which is of two types.

(a) Kinetic energy                     (b) Potential energy

Kinetic Energy : energy of doing work of an object by virtue of its motion.

$K.E. = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2$

Relation Between Kinetic Energy & Momentum

$K.E. = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$

$K\propto p^2$

For small changes (< 5%)

$\dfrac{\Delta K}{K} = 2 \dfrac{\Delta p}{p}$

As mass $m$ and $v^2$are always positive so K.E. can never be negative.

The kinetic energy depends on the frame of reference as v depends on the frame of reference.

The expression $KE = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2$ holds even when the force applied varies in magnitude or in direction or in both.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Work Energy Theorem:

The Work-Energy Theorem states that the work done by the net force on an object equals change in its kinetic energy. (or in other words, work done by all the forces on a system is equal to change in its kinetic energy

$W_{\text{all}} = \Delta KE$

$W_{\text{all}} = K_f - K_i = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2 - \dfrac{1}{2} m u^2$

Steps To Apply Work Energy Theorem:

• Identify the initial and final positions as position 1 and 2 and write expressions for kinetic energies, whether known or unknown.
    • Draw the free body diagram of the body at any intermediate stage between positions 1 and 2. The forces shown will help in deciding their work. Calculate work by each force and add them to obtain the total work done by all the forces.

• Use the work obtained in step 2 and kinetic energies obtained in step 1 in the equation.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: A particle of mass m moves with velocity $v = a \sqrt{x}$ where a is a constant. Find the total work done by all the forces during a displacement from $x = 0 $ to $ x = d.$
blocks.answer:
Work done by all forces

$W = \Delta KE = \dfrac{1}{2} m v_2^2 - \dfrac{1}{2} m v_1^2$

$v_1 = a \sqrt{0}, \quad v_2 = a \sqrt{d}$

$W = \frac{1}{2} m a^2d - 0$

$W = \frac{1}{2} m a^2 d$
blocks.prompt: A particle of mass m moves with velocity $v = a \sqrt{x}$ where a is a constant. Find the total work done by all the forces during a displacement from $x = 0 $ to $ x = d.$

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: Example:- A bullet weighing 10 g is fired with a velocity 800 m/s. It's velocity decreases to 100 m/s after passing through a 1m thick mud wall. Find the average resistance offered by the mud wall.
blocks.answer:
Solution:

Work done by the average resistance (offered by the wall) = change in K.E. of the bullet.

$F_s = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2 - \dfrac{1}{2} m u^2 \Rightarrow F = \dfrac{m(v^2 - u^2)}{2s} = \dfrac{0.01(100^2 - 800^2)}{2 \times 1} = -3150 \, \text{N}$

Resistance offered = 3150 N.

• Ignoring non-conservative forces.
    • Incorrect direction of forces.
    • Forgetting about work done by multiple forces.
    • Incorrectly applying kinetic energy expressions.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Conservative Forces:

A force is said to be conservative if the work done by the force is independent of the path and depends only on initial and final positions.

• work done over a closed path is ZERO.

• $W_1 = W_2 = W_3$

  • Examples: Gravitational force, electrostatic force, spring force etc.
  • Potential energy can only be defined for conservative forces.
  • Central Force: A force whose line of action always passes through a fixed point (which is known as centre of force) and whose magnitude depends only on the distance from this point is known as central force.
  • All forces following inverse square law are called central forces.
  • All central forces are conservative forces.
  • Central forces are functions of position only.
Non-Conservative Forces: A force is said to be non–conservative if work done by the force in moving a body depends upon the path between the initial and final positions.

  • Involves energy dissipation
  • Examples: Friction, air resistance, viscous force etc.
  • Potential energy can not be defined for non-conservative forces.

rows: Work done does not depend upon path.
Work done depends upon path.
Work done in a round trip is zero e.g. gravitational force
Work done in a round trip is not zero e.g. friction
Central forces, spring forces etc. are conservative forces
Forces which are velocity-dependent in nature e.g. dragging force, viscous force, etc.
When a conservative force acts within a system, the kinetic energy and potential energy can change. However, their sum, the mechanical energy of the system, does not change.
Work done against a non-conservative force may be dissipated as heat energy.
Work done is completely reversible.
Work done is not completely reversible.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: Why does friction not have a potential energy function?
blocks.answer: Friction is a non-conservative force, meaning the work done by friction depends on the path taken. Since friction dissipates energy (usually converting kinetic energy into heat), it cannot be associated with potential energy. Potential energy is only defined for conservative forces where the work done depends only on the position, not the path.
blocks.prompt: Why does friction not have a potential energy function?

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: A 5 kg object is moving on a flat horizontal surface. If the object is subjected to a constant frictional force of 10 N, how much energy is dissipated by friction after the object moves 20 meters?
blocks.answer:
The work done by friction is given by:

$W_{\text{friction}} = F_{\text{friction}} \times d \times \cos(\theta)$

$W_{\text{friction}} = 10 \times 20 \times \cos(180^\circ) = 10 \times 20 \times (-1) = -200 \, \text{J}$

blocks.title: Example-3
blocks.question: Can you have non-conservative forces in a system with no friction?
blocks.answer: Yes, non-conservative forces are not limited to friction. For example, forces like air resistance, tension, or applied forces that change the energy in ways other than by simple motion along a potential energy curve are non-conservative.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Potential Energy: The energy possessed by a body by virtue of its position or configuration in a conservative force field. Potential energy is a relative quantity.

Potential energy is defined only for conservative force field.

Relationship between conservative force field and potential energy:

$\vec{F}=-\nabla U=-\operatorname{grad} U$$=-\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial x} \hat{i}-\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial y} \hat{j}-\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial z} \hat{k}$

If force varies with only one dimension (say along x-axis) then

$F = -\dfrac{dU}{dx} \implies dU = -F \, dx$

$\implies \int_{U_1}^{U_2} dU = -\int_{x_1}^{x_2} F \, dx \implies \Delta U = -W_C$

Potential energy may be positive or negative or even zero.

  • Potential energy is positive, if the force field is repulsive in nature.
  • Potential energy is negative, if the force field is attractive in nature.
  • PE increases , when positive work is done by the external force (against the conservative force)
  • PE decreases , when positive work is done by the conservative force.
Gravitational Potential Energy: When a body is taken against Earth's Gravitational Force then work done by the weight on the body,

$\Delta U = U_f - U_i = mgh$

Spring Potential Energy: Work done by spring force depends only on initial and final position

$U_s = -W_s = \dfrac{1}{2} k \left( x_f^2 - x_i^2 \right)$

$x_f$ and $x_i$ are measured from natural length of spring.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.question: The potential energy of a particle of mass 1 kg free to move along the x-axis is given by  $\mathrm{U}(\mathrm{x})=\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{x}^2}{2}-\mathrm{x}\right)$ joules. If total mechanical energy of the particle is 2 J, then find its maximum speed.
blocks.answer:
$\text { Potential energy } \mathrm{U}=\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{x}^2}{2}-\mathrm{x}\right)$

$\text { For minimum } \mathrm{U}, \dfrac{\mathrm{dU}}{\mathrm{dx}}=\dfrac{2 \mathrm{x}}{2}-1=0 \text { and } \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2 \mathrm{U}}{\mathrm{dx}^2}=1=\text { positive }$

$\text { So, at } \mathrm{x}=1, \mathrm{U} \text { is minimum. Hence } \mathrm{U}_{\min }=-\dfrac{1}{2} \mathrm{~J} \text {. }$

$\text { Total mechanical energy }=\text { Max KE }+ \text { Min PE }$

$\begin{aligned} & 2=\dfrac{1}{2} m v^2+\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ & 2+\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{1}{2} m v^2 \\ & \dfrac{5}{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}(1)^2 v^2 \\ & v=\sqrt{5} m / s \end{aligned}$

modules.name: Equilibrium and Law of Conservation of Mechanical Energy

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Equilibrium: At equilibrium net force is zero. If net force acting on a body is zero then the body is said to be in equilibrium and positions where body achieves equilibrium are called equilibrium position.

$\text { At equilibrium, } \mathrm{F=-\dfrac{d U}{d x}=0}$

Potential Energy Curve

It is a curve which shows the change in potential energy with the position of a particle.

Stable Equilibrium

After a particle is slightly displaced from its equilibrium position if it tends to come back towards equilibrium due to restoring force then it is said to be in stable equilibrium.

Restoring Force is a force which acts to bring a body to its equilibrium position.

At point A : Slope $\mathrm{\dfrac{dU}{dx}}$ is negative so F is positive

At point C : Slope is positive so F is negative

At point B : It is the point of stable equilibrium

At point B : $\mathrm{U}=\mathrm{U}_{\min } \Rightarrow \dfrac{\mathrm{dU}}{\mathrm{dx}}=0 \text { and } \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2 \mathrm{U}}{\mathrm{dx}^2}=\text { positive }$

Unstable Equilibrium

After a particle is slightly displaced from its equilibrium position, if it tends to move away from equilibrium position then it is said to be in unstable equilibrium.

At point D : Slope $\mathrm{\dfrac{dU}{dx}}$ is positive so F is negative

At point G : Slope $\mathrm{\dfrac{dU}{dx}}$ is negative so F is positive

At point E : It is the point of unstable equilibrium

At point E : $\mathrm{U}=\mathrm{U}_{\max } \Rightarrow \dfrac{\mathrm{dU}}{\mathrm{dx}}=0 \text { and } \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2 \mathrm{U}}{\mathrm{dx}^2}=\text {negative }$

Neutral Equilibrium

After a particle is slightly displaced from its equilibrium position if no force acts on it then the equilibrium is said to be neutral equilibrium.

Point H corresponds to neutral equilibrium

$\Rightarrow \mathrm{U}=\text { constant } ; \dfrac{\mathrm{dU}}{\mathrm{dx}}=0, \dfrac{\mathrm{~d}^2 \mathrm{U}}{\mathrm{dx}^2}=0$

Law of Conservation of Mechanical Energy

The total potential energy of a system and the total kinetic energy of all the constituent bodies together is known as the mechanical energy of the system. If E, K and U respectively denote the total mechanical energy, total kinetic energy and the total potential energy of a system in any configuration then we have

$ E = K + U  $

$K_1 + U_1 = K_2 + U_2$

$ E = K + U$=Constant

$\Delta E = 0 \implies \Delta K + \Delta U = 0$

blocks.title: Example
blocks.question: The P.E. for a conservative force system is given by $\mathrm{U}=\mathrm{a} \mathrm{x}^2-\mathrm{bx},$ where a and b are constants. Find out the (a) expression for force (b) potential energy at equilibrium.
blocks.answer:
(a) For Conservative Force F$=-\dfrac{d U}{d x}=-(2 a x-b)=-2 a x+b$   &   for Equilibrium F = 0, $x=\frac{b}{2 a}$

(b) $ U=a\left(\dfrac{b}{2 a}\right)^2-b\left(\dfrac{b}{2 a}\right)=\dfrac{b^2}{4 a}-\dfrac{b^2}{2 a}=-\dfrac{b^2}{4 a}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Power: It is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred over time.

$P = \frac{{Work\,done(W)}}{{Time\,\operatorname{int} erval(\Delta t)}}$

Instantaneous Power : It is the scalar product of force and velocity at a particular instant.

$P = \dfrac{dW}{dt}$=$\dfrac{\vec{F} \cdot \vec{dr}}{dt}$=$\vec{F} \cdot \vec{v}$

Power is a scalar quantity with dimensions:

[ M1L2T–3 ]

SI unit : -  J/s or watt

1 horsepower = 746 watts

Graphical Analysis : Area under power-time graph gives the work done

$W = \int P \, dt$

Efficiency: Efficiency of a machine denote how much a machine is effective in converting energy into useful work.

$\eta = \dfrac{\text{Work Done}}{\text{Energy Input}}$

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: A small motor is used to power a lift that raises a load of bricks weighing 800N to a height of 20m in 40s. What is the minimum power motor needed?
blocks.answer:
Assuming that the bricks are lifted without acceleration, the upwards force equal to the force of gravity 800N.

$\begin{aligned} P=\frac{m g h}{t}= & \frac{800 \times 20}{40} \\ & =400 \mathrm{~W}\end{aligned}$

If there are no energy losses, e.g. to frictional forces, the motor must have a power output of 400W
blocks.prompt: A small motor is used to power a lift that raises a load of bricks weighing 800N to a height of 20m in 40s. What is the minimum power motor needed?

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: A pump can take out 7200 kg of water per hour from a 100 m deep well. Calculate the power of the pump, assuming that its efficiency is 50%. (g = 10 m/s2)
blocks.answer:
Output power =$\dfrac{mgh}{t} = \dfrac{7200 \times 10 \times 100}{3600} = 2000 \, \text{W}$

$\eta = \dfrac{\text{output power}}{\text{ Input power}}$

$\text{Input Power} = \dfrac{\text{Output Power}}{\eta}$=$\dfrac{2000 \times 100}{50} = 4000 \, \text{W} = 4 \, \text{kW}$
blocks.prompt: A pump can take out 7200 kg of water per hour from a 100 m deep well. Calculate the power of the pump, assuming that its efficiency is 50%. (g = 10 m/s2)

blocks.title: Example-3
blocks.question:
Example :-An engine pumps water of density $\rho$,through a hose pipe. Water leaves the hose pipe of cross-sectional area $A$ with a velocity $v$. Find the

(1) Rate at which kinetic energy is imparted to water

(2) power of the engine.
blocks.answer:
(1) Rate of change of kinetic energy

$\dfrac{\mathrm{dE}_{\mathrm{k}}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{dt}}\left(\dfrac{1}{2} m v^2\right)=\dfrac{1}{2} v^2 \dfrac{\mathrm{dm}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\dfrac{1}{2} \mathrm{v}^2 \dfrac{\mathrm{~d}}{\mathrm{dt}}(\rho A x)$$=\frac{1}{2} \rho A v^2 \frac{d x}{d t}=\frac{1}{2} \rho A v^3$

(2) Power=$\mathrm{Fv}=\left(\mathrm{v} \dfrac{\mathrm{dm}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right) \mathrm{v}=\mathrm{v}^2 \dfrac{\mathrm{dm}}{\mathrm{dt}}$$=v^2(\rho A v)=\rho A v^3$
options: (1) Rate at which kinetic energy is imparted to water

Potential Energy: The energy possessed by a body by virtue of its position or configuration in a conservative force field. Potential energy is a relative quantity.

Potential energy is defined only for conservative force field.

Relationship between conservative force field and potential energy:

$\vec{F}=-\nabla U=-\operatorname{grad} U$$=-\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial x} \hat{i}-\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial y} \hat{j}-\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial z} \hat{k}$

If force varies with only one dimension (say along x-axis) then

$F = -\dfrac{dU}{dx} \implies dU = -F \, dx$

$\implies \int_{U_1}^{U_2} dU = -\int_{x_1}^{x_2} F \, dx \implies \Delta U = -W_C$

Potential energy may be positive or negative or even zero.

  • Potential energy is positive, if the force field is repulsive in nature.
  • Potential energy is negative, if the force field is attractive in nature.
  • PE increases , when positive work is done by the external force (against the conservative force)
  • PE decreases , when positive work is done by the conservative force.
Gravitational Potential Energy: When a body is taken against Earth's Gravitational Force then work done by the weight on the body,

$\Delta U = U_f - U_i = mgh$

Spring Potential Energy: Work done by spring force depends only on initial and final position

$U_s = -W_s = \dfrac{1}{2} k \left( x_f^2 - x_i^2 \right)$

$x_f$ and $x_i$ are measured from natural length of spring.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Equilibrium: At equilibrium net force is zero. If net force acting on a body is zero then the body is said to be in equilibrium and positions where body achieves equilibrium are called equilibrium position.

$\text { At equilibrium, } \mathrm{F=-\dfrac{d U}{d x}=0}$

Potential Energy Curve

It is a curve which shows the change in potential energy with the position of a particle.

Stable Equilibrium

After a particle is slightly displaced from its equilibrium position if it tends to come back towards equilibrium due to restoring force then it is said to be in stable equilibrium.

Restoring Force is a force which acts to bring a body to its equilibrium position.

At point A : Slope $\mathrm{\dfrac{dU}{dx}}$ is negative so F is positive

At point C : Slope is positive so F is negative

At point B : It is the point of stable equilibrium

At point B : $\mathrm{U}=\mathrm{U}_{\min } \Rightarrow \dfrac{\mathrm{dU}}{\mathrm{dx}}=0 \text { and } \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2 \mathrm{U}}{\mathrm{dx}^2}=\text { positive }$

Unstable Equilibrium

After a particle is slightly displaced from its equilibrium position, if it tends to move away from equilibrium position then it is said to be in unstable equilibrium.

At point D : Slope $\mathrm{\dfrac{dU}{dx}}$ is positive so F is negative

At point G : Slope $\mathrm{\dfrac{dU}{dx}}$ is negative so F is positive

At point E : It is the point of unstable equilibrium

At point E : $\mathrm{U}=\mathrm{U}_{\max } \Rightarrow \dfrac{\mathrm{dU}}{\mathrm{dx}}=0 \text { and } \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2 \mathrm{U}}{\mathrm{dx}^2}=\text {negative }$

Neutral Equilibrium

After a particle is slightly displaced from its equilibrium position if no force acts on it then the equilibrium is said to be neutral equilibrium.

Point H corresponds to neutral equilibrium

$\Rightarrow \mathrm{U}=\text { constant } ; \dfrac{\mathrm{dU}}{\mathrm{dx}}=0, \dfrac{\mathrm{~d}^2 \mathrm{U}}{\mathrm{dx}^2}=0$

Law of Conservation of Mechanical Energy

The total potential energy of a system and the total kinetic energy of all the constituent bodies together is known as the mechanical energy of the system. If E, K and U respectively denote the total mechanical energy, total kinetic energy and the total potential energy of a system in any configuration then we have

$ E = K + U  $

$K_1 + U_1 = K_2 + U_2$

$ E = K + U$=Constant

$\Delta E = 0 \implies \Delta K + \Delta U = 0$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Power: It is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred over time.

$P = \frac{{Work\,done(W)}}{{Time\,\operatorname{int} erval(\Delta t)}}$

Instantaneous Power : It is the scalar product of force and velocity at a particular instant.

$P = \dfrac{dW}{dt}$=$\dfrac{\vec{F} \cdot \vec{dr}}{dt}$=$\vec{F} \cdot \vec{v}$

Power is a scalar quantity with dimensions:

[ M1L2T–3 ]

SI unit : -  J/s or watt

1 horsepower = 746 watts

Graphical Analysis : Area under power-time graph gives the work done

$W = \int P \, dt$

Efficiency: Efficiency of a machine denote how much a machine is effective in converting energy into useful work.

$\eta = \dfrac{\text{Work Done}}{\text{Energy Input}}$

rows: Work done does not depend upon path.
Work done depends upon path.
Work done in a round trip is zero e.g. gravitational force
Work done in a round trip is not zero e.g. friction
Central forces, spring forces etc. are conservative forces
Forces which are velocity-dependent in nature e.g. dragging force, viscous force, etc.
When a conservative force acts within a system, the kinetic energy and potential energy can change. However, their sum, the mechanical energy of the system, does not change.
Work done against a non-conservative force may be dissipated as heat energy.
Work done is completely reversible.
Work done is not completely reversible.
